The text reaches an extension request only through "applicant," which Section 2 defines as a "registered participant," and Section 1 confines the whole chapter to registered participants. ## Lens 2 - How Each Side Argues It

### Our best reading (Taylor may request)

Taylor wins if registered. Sections 2 and 3 together give "an applicant" the ability to request an extension, and a registered participant who seeks one is an applicant by definition. If Taylor is not registered, Taylor's best argument is Section 4: the chapter must be "liberally construed to permit access to its review process," and a request for an extension is the entry point to review. Taylor would also argue that an excluded person is the very person to whom "access" most matters, and that the staff email shows an inclusive purpose. The staff email is weak because it is not enacted.

### Their best reading (Taylor may not request)

If Taylor is not registered, then Section 1 ("applies only to registered participants") and Section 2 (applicant means a "registered participant") make the chapter inapplicable. Section 4 directs how to construe what the chapter says. It does not purport to remove the word "only" or to amend the definition of "applicant." A liberal-construction directive that overrode an express coverage limit would make Section 1 meaningless, which the surplusage canon disfavors. The email is not law.

If Taylor is registered, the opposing side's strongest point is not that Taylor cannot request but that Section 3 says "may." The chapter states no standard for granting an extension, so a grant is not assured. That is a different question from whether a request may be made. The opposing side might also say that "registered" has an undefined meaning (registered with whom, and as of when) and that mere enrollment in something else is not registration under this chapter.

### Best contrary reading, at full strength

Taylor is entitled to ask, whether or not registered. Section 4 commands liberal construction "to permit access," and an applicant's "access" to review begins with the request itself. Reading Section 1 as a hard wall would let a coverage clause defeat the purpose Section 4 states in the chapter's own words. Section 3 gives no express limit on who can send a request, and the legislature knew how to say "only" because it did in Section 1. Taylor would add that excluding a person from asking, as opposed to being granted, adds nothing to the chapter's purpose. Why the adopted reading is stronger: Section 4 tells a reader how to resolve doubt about what the chapter means, and it identifies "its review process" as the object of access. The "only" in Section 1 and the definition in Section 2 are not doubtful, and reading Section 4 to erase them would leave Section 1's limiting word with no function. The contrary reading is still live and has not been eliminated. It would be strengthened if the rest of the chapter shows that an unregistered person has some path into the process.
